$$
-7{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+2x{y}^{′}+(x-5)y=0
$$

Find the indicial equation for a Frobenius series solution about the regular singular point $x=0$ of the differential equation above.
fields.source_quote:
If $x=0$ is a regular singular point of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation, then the method of Frobenius states that there is at least one solution of the form

$$
y={x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n},
$$

where $\lambda $ and ${a}_{n}$ for $n=0,1,2,…$ are constants.

Substituting this solution and its derivatives into the ODE, collecting like terms, and setting coefficients equal to zero, we obtain: 

- the indicial equation from the coefficients of the $n=0$ term for arbitrary ${a}_{0},$ and

- a recurrence formula from the coefficients of the $n\ge 1$ terms.

**Step 1**: Write the solution $y$ as a Frobenius power series:

$$
y={x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n}={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the derivatives ${y}^{′}$ and ${y}^{″}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-1}, \\ {y}^{″} & ={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(\lambda +n-1)(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Rewrite all the series so that they use the same index of summation.

The terms of the differential equation are

$$
\begin{aligned}-7{x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =-7{x}^{2}\cdot {\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(\lambda +n-1)(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-2} \\  & =-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }7((\lambda +n)^{2}-(\lambda +n)){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}, \\ 2x{y}^{′} & =2x\cdot {\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-1} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }2(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}, \\ (x-5)y & =(x-5){\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n+1}-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }5{a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}.\end{aligned}
$$

In the first sum of the $y$ term, we change the index of the summation by writing $m=n+1.$ This gives

$$
(x-5)y={\sum }_{m=1}^{\infty }{a}_{m-1}{x}^{\lambda +m}-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }5{a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}.
$$

Then, replacing $m$ with $n$ (since it does not matter which letter we use) and isolating the $n=0$ term gives

$$
(x-5)y={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n-1}{x}^{\lambda +n}-5{a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }5{a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}.
$$

Similarly, isolating the $n=0$ terms for the other terms in the ODE, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-7{x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =-7({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }7((\lambda +n)^{2}-(\lambda +n)){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}, \\ 2x{y}^{′} & =2\lambda {a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }2(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Consolidate all the series into a single series that is equal to $0.$

Collecting the terms for $n=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-7({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+2\lambda {a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }-5{a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda } & = \\ (-7{\lambda }^{2}+7\lambda +2\lambda -5){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda } & = \\ (-7{\lambda }^{2}+9\lambda -5){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }. & \end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, collecting terms for $n\ge 1,$ we obtain an infinite series of the form
${x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(\lambda ){x}^{n},$
for some ${b}_{n}(\lambda ),$ $n\ge 1.$
Therefore, substituting into the homogeneous ODE, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(-7{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -5){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(\lambda ){x}^{n} & =0 \\ (-7{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -5){a}_{0}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(\lambda ){x}^{n} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5**:  Set the coefficients of the series equal to $0.$

Setting the coefficient of the $n=0$ term equal to $0$ with arbitrary ${a}_{0}\ne 0,$ we obtain the indicial equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-7{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -5){a}_{0} & =0 \\ 7{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

supporting_evidence.prompt: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}=1$ at the point $(0,0,2).$
supporting_evidence.worked_solution:
First, note that we can write the equation of our surface as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,0,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,0,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1)k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+\frac{2y}{9}\text{ }j+\frac{z}{2}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,0,2) & =2(0)\text{ }i+\frac{2(0)}{9}\text{ }j+\frac{(2)}{2}\text{ }k \\  & =k \\  & =⟨0,0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, the vector form of the equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(0,0,2)$ and passes through the point $(0,0,2)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨0,\,0,\,2⟩+t\,∇f(0,0,2)=⟨0,\,0,\,2⟩+t\,⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
fields.source_quote:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

fields.binding:
A rock of mass $2\,\text{kg}$ falls vertically downward. Let $v(t)$ be the rock's velocity, in meters per second, $t\ge 0$ seconds after the fall began, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the rock is proportional to the square of the rock's velocity and acts in the direction opposite to motion.

Which differential equation best models the velocity? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, the acceleration due to gravity is $g,$ and the only forces acting on the rock are the weight due to gravity and drag.
fields.source_quote:
Recall Newton's second law, which states that the resultant force $F$ acting on a body equals the product of its mass $m$ and acceleration $a:$

$$
F=ma
$$

In our case, two forces are acting on the rock:

- The force due to gravity, given by the weight $w$ of the rock, which equals

$$
\begin{aligned}w & =mg \\  & =2g.\end{aligned}
$$

- The force due to drag (air resistance) $D,$ which is proportional to the square of the velocity of the rock (and negative since it acts in the negative direction):

$$
D=-k{v}^{2},
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Note that, since drag, in $\text{N}=\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m/s}}^{2},$ is the product of the constant $k$ and squared velocity, in $(\text{m/s})^{2}={\text{m}}^{2}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ the units of $k$ are

$$
\frac{\text{N}}{{\text{m}}^{2}/{\text{s}}^{2}}=\frac{\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m/s}}^{2}}{{\text{m}}^{2}/{\text{s}}^{2}}=\text{kg/m}.
$$

Summing the forces, the resultant force acting on the rock is

$$
F=w+D=2g-k{v}^{2}.
$$

Also, recall that acceleration is the derivative of velocity: $a=\frac{dv}{dt}.$
Substituting this into Newton's second law, along with our expression for the resultant force on the rock, we get

$$
2g-k{v}^{2}=2\,\frac{dv}{dt}\,⟹\,\frac{dv}{dt}=g-\frac{k}{2}{v}^{2}.
$$

fields.binding: The equation ${z}^{2}-50=-10z$ can be written in the form $(z+p{)}^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q,$ and solve the equation.
fields.source_quote:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, the $-10z$ term to the left-hand side, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2}-50 & =-10z \\ {z}^{2}+10z & =50 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot 5\cdot z & =50 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot 5\cdot z+{5}^{2}-{5}^{2} & =50 \\ (z+5{)}^{2}-{5}^{2} & =50\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(z+5{)}^{2}-{5}^{2} & =50 \\ (z+5{)}^{2} & =75\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=5,q=75,$ and $p+q=80.$

Next, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(z+5{)}^{2} & =75 \\ \sqrt{(z+5{)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{75} \\ |z+5| & =\sqrt{75} \\ z+5 & =\pm 5\sqrt{3} \\ z & =-5\pm 5\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
Consider the following differential equation.

$$
16{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+(x-5)x{y}^{′}+(5+2x)y=0
$$

The general solution near $x=0$ of the differential equation is given by

$$
y={c}_{1}{y}_{1}(x)+{c}_{2}{y}_{2}(x),
$$

where ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ are arbitrary constants and ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are linearly independent solutions. According to the Frobenius method, what is the best choice for the first solution ${y}_{1},$ where ${a}_{n}$ for $n=0,1,2,…$ are constants determined by substitution?

*Hint: You may assume $x=0$ is a regular singular point of the ODE and the indicial equation of the ODE is $16{\lambda }^{2}-21\lambda +5=0.$*
fields.source_quote:
The general solution near a regular singular point $x=0$ of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation with indicial roots ${\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}$ is given by

$$
y={c}_{1}{y}_{1}(x)+{c}_{2}{y}_{2}(x),
$$

where

- ${y}_{1}(x)={x}^{{\lambda }_{1}}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}({\lambda }_{1}){x}^{n}$ is the first Frobenius solution corresponding to the larger root of the indicial equation, and

- ${a}_{n}({\lambda }_{1})$ are the coefficients produced by the method when $\lambda ={\lambda }_{1}.$

We are given that the indicial equation is $16{\lambda }^{2}-21\lambda +5=0.$
Solving for the roots, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}16{\lambda }^{2}-21\lambda +5 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(16\lambda -5) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =\frac{5}{16},1\end{aligned}
$$

The larger solution is ${\lambda }_{1}=1.$ Therefore, the first Frobenius series solution we take is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={x}^{1}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n}=x{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n}.
$$

fields.binding:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
fields.source_quote:
Notice that the matrix $M$ is already in row echelon form. The system corresponding to $M$ is 

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+0y+3z=7 \\ 0x+y+2z=-3 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final equation $0x+0y+0z=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of just two equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+3z=7 \\ y+2z=-3\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are $x$ and $y,$ and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$ To do this, we apply the back substitution. 

From the first equation, we get

$$
x+3z=7\,⇒\,x=7-3z
$$

and from the second equation, we obtain

$$
y+2z=-3\,⇒\,y=-3-2z.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=7-3z \\ y=-3-2z \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

where $z$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}7-3z \\ -3-2z \\ z\end{aligned}],\,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding: The velocity $v$ of a merry-go-round decreases at a rate that is proportional to the velocity at that moment. What differential equation describes the rate of change of the velocity at time $t?$
fields.source_quote:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **velocity** $v$ of a merry-go-round **decreases** at a **rate** that is **proportional** to the **velocity** at the moment.* 

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *velocity* of a merry-go-round 
varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ is *proportional to* the *velocity.* In other words,

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}∝v.
$$

Recall that $∝$ means "is proportional to."

- Finally, we want to replace the proportionality symbol with an equality symbol. Let $k$ be a positive constant. Since the velocity *decreases* with time, our derivative should be *negative*. Therefore, we can rewrite our proportionality statement as

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-kv.
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are $x$ and $y,$ and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$

$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $cos⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $cos⁡\theta $ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $cos⁡\theta =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$

Finally, knowing that $tan⁡\theta =\frac{sin⁡\theta }{cos⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
tan⁡\theta =\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.
$$

The sides of a square decrease in length at a rate of $2\text{ m/s}.$ At what rate is the area of the square decreasing when the sides are $10\text{ m}$ long?
fields.source_quote:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each side of the square is decreasing at a rate of $2\,\text{m/s},$ so we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-2.$ Also, when the sides are $10\,\text{m},$ we have $x=10.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =(-2)\cdot 2(10)=-40{\text{ m}}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square decreases at $40\,{\text{m}}^{2}/\text{s}.$

fields.binding: The equation $-20{x}^{2}+60x-41=0$ can be written in the form $20(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q,$ and solve the equation.
fields.source_quote:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-20{x}^{2}+60x-41) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 20{x}^{2}-60x+41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}20{x}^{2}-60x+41 & =0 \\ 20{x}^{2}-60x & =-41 \\ 20({x}^{2}-3x) & =-41 \\ 20[{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}] & =-41 \\ 20[{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4}] & =-41\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-20\cdot \frac{9}{4} & =-41 \\ 20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-45 & =-41 \\ 20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =45-41 \\ 20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q=4.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4 \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{4}{20} \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{5} \\ \sqrt{{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{5}} \\ |x-\frac{3}{2}| & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{5}} \\ x-\frac{3}{2} & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ x-\frac{3}{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma 
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta ,$ and $\gamma $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x+\beta ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=2\alpha 
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ $\beta $ and $\gamma ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
2\alpha +4(2\alpha x+\beta )-12(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma )=12{x}^{2}-32x-30
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives:

$$
-12\alpha {x}^{2}+(8\alpha -12\beta )x+(2\alpha +4\beta -12\gamma )=12{x}^{2}-32x-30
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$

$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-1,\beta =2,\gamma =3.$

Therefore, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$

\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-6}-\frac{1}{s}} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-6}}-{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s}} \\  & ={e}^{6t}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the inverse Laplace transform of $F(s)=\frac{6}{{s}^{2}-6s}$ is $f(t)={e}^{6t}-1.$

fields.binding: Given that ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}$ is a solution to the equation ${y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+y=0,$ use reduction of order to find a second solution ${y}_{2}(x)$ to the equation.
fields.source_quote:
According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x){e}^{x}.$ 

Differentiating the above with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x}={e}^{x}({u}^{′}+u) \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={e}^{x}({u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}+u).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}({u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}+u)-2{e}^{x}({u}^{′}+u)+{e}^{x}(u) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}+u-2{u}^{′}-2u+u) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}{u}^{″} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{x}\ne 0$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}=0\,⟹\,w={c}_{1}.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}\,⟹\,u={c}_{1}x+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u{e}^{x}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{x}({c}_{1}x+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{x}\cdot x=x{e}^{x}.
$$

fields.binding: Given that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ evaluate ${f}_{yxx}(1,1)$ if ${f}_{xy}(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}(2+xy).$
fields.source_quote:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yxx}(x,y) & ={f}_{xyx}(x,y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{xy}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{xy}(2+xy)) \\  & ={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}(2+xy)+{y}^{2}{e}^{xy} \\  & ={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}(3+xy).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,1):$

$$
{f}_{yxx}(1,1)=(1)^{2}{e}^{1\cdot 1}(3+(1)(1))=4e\,\,
$$

fields.binding: The equation ${x}^{2}+16x+164=0$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q,$ and solve the equation.

We first move the constant to the right-hand side:

$$

Next, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+16x & =-164 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 8x+{8}^{2}-{8}^{2} & =-164 \\ (x+8)^{2}-64 & =-164 \\ (x+8)^{2} & =-100\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=8,\,q=-100,$ and $p+q=-92.$

We now solve the equation using the square root method.

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+8)^{2} & =-100 \\ x+8 & =\pm \sqrt{-100} \\ x+8 & =\pm 10\,\text{i} \\ x & =-8\pm 10\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, $x=-8+10\,\text{i}$ and $x=-8-10\,\text{i}.$

fields.binding: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $z=2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x$ at the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$
fields.source_quote:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x \\ z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(\frac{1}{2},1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)k \\  & =(-4x-1)\text{ }i-4y\text{ }j+k \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3) & =(-4(\frac{1}{2})-1)\,i-4(1)\text{ }j+k \\  & =-3\,i-4\,j+k \\  & =⟨-3,-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ and passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨-3,-4,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

fields.binding:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)=-\frac{2}{9}{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}+14t+17,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
fields.source_quote:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{2}{9}{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}+14t+17) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{t}^{2}+6t+14\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{2}{3}{t}^{2}+6t+14) \\  & =-\frac{4}{3}t+6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-\frac{4}{3}t+6 \\ \frac{4}{3}t & =6 \\ t & =4.5\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t=4.5.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
v(4.5)=-\frac{2}{3}(4.5)^{2}+6(4.5)+14=27.5.
$$

fields.binding: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=4-{t}^{2}$, where $t>0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
fields.source_quote:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 4-{t}^{2} & =0 \\ (2-t)(2+t) & =0 \\ t & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t⩾0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-{t}^{2}) \\  & =-2t \\ {v}^{″}(2) & =-2(2) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(2)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (4-{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =4t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4(0)-\frac{1}{3}(0)^{3}+C & =0 \\ 0+0+C & =0\,⟹\,C=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=4t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(2)=4(2)-\frac{1}{3}(2)^{3}=\frac{16}{3}\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$
fields.method: Full worked solution and prompt reviewed; original option matches the requested mathematical conclusion, with independent arithmetic/sign/domain check.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨6t-2,4⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (6t-2)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}-2t+{C}_{1},\,4t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨1,4⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨3(1)^{2}-2(1)+{C}_{1},\,4(1)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,4⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},4+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨3{t}^{2}-2t,\,4t⟩.\end{aligned}

fields.binding: Calculate the points where the ellipse $2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-20x+6y+47=0$ intercepts the $x$-axis.
fields.source_quote:
To calculate the $x$-intercepts, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ We do this and solve the resulting equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-20x+6y+47 & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}+3(0)^{2}-20x+6(0)+47 & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-20x+47 & =0 \\ 2[{x}^{2}-10x]+47 & =0 \\ 2[(x-5)^{2}-25]+47 & =0 \\ 2(x-5)^{2}-50+47 & =0 \\ 2(x-5)^{2} & =3 \\ (x-5)^{2} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ x-5 & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} \\ x & =5\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at $(5-\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}},0)$ and $(5+\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}},0).$

fields.binding: The displacement $s,$ in meters, relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t)=t{e}^{-2t}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time, measured in seconds. Find the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x.$
fields.source_quote:
If the particle moves in the direction of increasing $x,$ then its velocity is positive. 

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t{e}^{-2t}) \\  & ={e}^{-2t}(1-2t)\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x$, we solve $v(t)>0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & >0 \\ {e}^{-2t}(1-2t) & >0 \\ 1-2t & >0 \\ 2t & <1 \\ t & <\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of increasing $x$ is $t\in [0,\frac{1}{2}).$

$$

Substituting the above into the given equation  $\text{d}(x,y)=2\sqrt{3},$ we obtain an equation that we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{6{k}^{2}-8k+14} & =2\sqrt{3} \\ {(\sqrt{6{k}^{2}-8k+14})}^{2} & ={(2\sqrt{3})}^{2} \\ 6{k}^{2}-8k+14 & =12 \\ 6{k}^{2}-8k+2 & =0 \\ 3{k}^{2}-4k+1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the quadratic formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}k & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-(-4)\pm \sqrt{(-4)^{2}-4(3)(1)}}{2(3)} \\  & =\frac{4\pm \sqrt{4}}{6} \\  & =\frac{4\pm 2}{6} \\  & =\frac{2\pm 1}{3},\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ {E}_{1}A & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={t}^{4}-3{t}^{2},\,y=2{t}^{3}-t,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=1$ on the curve. Find the equation of the normal to the curve at $C.$
fields.source_quote:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(1)^{4}-3(1)^{2}=-2, \\ y & =2(1)^{3}-1=1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the normal at the point $(-2,1).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4{t}^{3}-6t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=6{t}^{2}-1.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{6{t}^{2}-1}{4{t}^{3}-6t}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$  the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =\frac{6(1)^{2}-1}{4(1)^{3}-6(1)} \\  & =\frac{5}{-2} \\  & =-\,\frac{5}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(\,-\frac{5}{2}\,)}=\frac{2}{5}
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-2,1)$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=\frac{2}{5}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =\frac{2}{5}(x+2) \\ y & =\frac{2}{5}(x+2)+1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

*The rate of growth of a **car's displacement** $D(t)$ **increases** at a **rate** that's **proportional** to the **time** $t$ since the car started moving.*

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *car's displacement* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}$ is *proportional to* the *interval of time* since the car started moving. In other words,

$$
\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}∝t.
$$

Recall that $∝$ means "is proportional to."

- Finally, we want to replace the proportionality symbol with an equality symbol. Let $k$ be a positive constant. Since the car's displacement *increases* with time, our derivative should be *positive*. Therefore, we can rewrite our proportionality statement as

$$
\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}=kt.
$$

supporting_evidence.prompt:
Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=\pi $, in ascending powers of $(x-\pi )$ up to and including the term in $(x-\pi )^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}={y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,y(\pi )=1,\,{y}^{′}(\pi )=-1.
$$
supporting_evidence.worked_solution:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=\pi $:

$$
y(x)=y(\pi )+(x-\pi ){y}^{′}(\pi )+\frac{(x-\pi )^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(\pi )+\frac{(x-\pi )^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(\pi )+⋯
$$

We're given $y(\pi )$ and ${y}^{′}(\pi ),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{″}(\pi )$ and ${y}^{(3)}(\pi ).$

We substitute $y(\pi )=1$ into the given equation to find ${y}^{″}(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(\pi ) & ={y}^{2}(\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot (0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate both sides on the given equation with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}(x)=2y{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{(3)}(\pi )$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(\pi ) & =2y(\pi ){y}^{′}(\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+{y}^{2}(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =2(1)(-1)(0)+(1)^{2}(-1) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we  substitute  the obtained values in  the Taylor series:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =y(\pi )+(x-\pi ){y}^{′}(\pi )+\frac{(x-\pi )^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(\pi )+\frac{(x-\pi )^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(\pi )+⋯ \\  & =1+(x-\pi )\cdot (-1)+\frac{(x-\pi )^{2}}{2}\cdot (0)+\frac{(x-\pi )^{3}}{6}\cdot (-1)+… \\  & =1-(x-\pi )-\frac{1}{6}(x-\pi )^{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Given that for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t$ for $s>0.$
fields.source_quote:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} & =L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}+L{3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} \\  & =L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}+3L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0, \\ L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4},\,s>0 \\ L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}+3L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}+3\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}+\frac{3s}{{s}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{3s+2}{{s}^{2}+4},\,s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=8x{y}^{1/2}-\frac{4}{x}y\,,\,y>0.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{1/2}.$*
fields.source_quote:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1/2}\,⟹\,y={z}^{2}\,.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{dz}{dx}=\frac{1}{2{y}^{1/2}}\frac{dy}{dx}\,⟹\,\frac{dy}{dx}=2z\frac{dz}{dx}.
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2z\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =8xz-\frac{4}{x}{z}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =4x-\frac{2}{x}z\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =4x-\frac{2}{x}z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z & =4x\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=4x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (4x) \\ {x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2xz & =4{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z) & =4{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z)\,\text{d}x & =\int 4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ {x}^{2}z & ={x}^{4}+C \\ z & =\frac{{x}^{4}+C}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{1/2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{1/2} & =\frac{{x}^{4}+C}{{x}^{2}} \\ y & =\frac{({x}^{4}+C)^{2}}{{x}^{4}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
(x+1)\frac{dy}{dx}=2{y}^{1/2}(x+1)^{3}+2y,\,y(0)=\frac{1}{4},\,x>-1.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z=(x+1)^{2}
$$

using the substitution $z={y}^{1/2}.$*
fields.source_quote:
The substitution $z={y}^{1/2}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z=(x+1)^{2},
$$

with the initial condition

$$
z(0)=\sqrt{y(0)}=\frac{1}{2}\,.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=-\frac{1}{x+1},\,Q(x)=(x+1)^{2}\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-\int 1/(x+1)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)^{-1}} \\  & =(x+1)^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x>-1.$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=(x+1)^{-1}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z) & =\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot (x+1)^{2} \\ \frac{1}{x+1}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\,z & =x+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x+1}\,z) & =x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x+1}\,z)\,\text{d}x & =\int (x+1)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{x+1}\,z & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+C \\ z & =(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+C)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we determine the value of $C$ that satisfies the initial condition $z(0)=\frac{1}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z(0) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ (0+1)(\frac{1}{2}{0}^{2}+0+C) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have 

$$
z=(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2})\,.
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by substituting the solution into $z={y}^{1/2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{1/2} & =(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2}) \\ y & =(x+1)^{2}{(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding:
Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=0$, in ascending powers of $x$ up to and including the term in ${x}^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=yx+{e}^{x},\,y(0)=0.
$$
fields.source_quote:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=0$:

$$
y(x)=y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯
$$

We're given $y(0),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{′}(0),$  ${y}^{″}(0)$ and ${y}^{(3)}(0).$

We know that $y(0)=0,$ so we substitute this into the given equation to find ${y}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =y(0)(0)+{e}^{0}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find an expression for ${y}^{″}(x),$ we differentiate both sides on the given equation with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{″}(x)={y}^{′}x+y+{e}^{x}
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{″}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(0) & ={y}^{′}(0)(0)+y(0)+{e}^{0} \\  & =0+0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

To find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate ${y}^{″}(x)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}(x)={y}^{″}x+{y}^{′}+{y}^{′}+{e}^{x}={y}^{″}x+2{y}^{′}+{e}^{x}
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{(3)}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(0) & ={y}^{″}(0)(0)+2{y}^{′}(0)+{e}^{0} \\  & =0+2(1)+1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we  substitute  the obtained values in  the Taylor series:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯ \\  & =0+x\cdot 1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\cdot 1+\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}\cdot 3+⋯ \\  & =x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=0$, in ascending powers of $x$ up to and including the term in ${x}^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$

fields.source_quote:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=0$:

$$
y(x)=y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯
$$

We're given $y(0),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{′}(0),$  ${y}^{″}(0)$ and ${y}^{(3)}(0).$

We know that $y(0)=-1,$ so we substitute this into the given equation to find ${y}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =2(0)-y(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(0) & =2-{y}^{′}(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0+y(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =2-(1)(1)+(-1)(0) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

To find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate ${y}^{″}(x)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}(x)=-{y}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x=-{y}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(0) & =-{y}^{″}(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0+2{y}^{′}(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡0+y(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =-(1)(1)+2(1)(0)+(-1)(1) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}

fields.binding:
Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}].$
fields.source_quote:
First, we find the matrix $\,A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is given by $det(A-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $1$st row, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-{\lambda }^{3}+6\lambda +5)-(-1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ -{\lambda }^{3}+7\lambda +6 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}-7\lambda -6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to solve this equation. We find the first root by testing some values. According to the rational zeros theorem, a list of good first guesses consists of all divisors of $6:$ 

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 3,\pm 6
$$

- Let's pick $x=1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)^{3}-7(1)-6 & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =1$ is not a root of the equation.

- Let's pick $x=-1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)^{3}-7(-1)-6 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =-1$ is a root of the equation.

So, we can factor $(\lambda +1)$ out of ${\lambda }^{3}-7\lambda -6$ using synthetic division:

| $-1$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-7$ | $-6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $↓$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $6$ |
|  | $1$ | $-1$ | $-6$ | $0$ |

So, we obtain the following factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +1)({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -6) & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=3.$

fields.binding: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2yx+y{x}^{2}$ that satisfies $y(1)=1.$
fields.source_quote:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2yx+y{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(2x+{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x+{x}^{2} \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =2\int x\,\text{d}x+\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & ={x}^{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ y & =\pm {e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ y & =K{e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(1)=1$ to find $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =1 \\ K{e}^{{1}^{2}+{1}^{3}/3} & =1 \\ K{e}^{4/3} & =1 \\ K & ={e}^{-4/3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2yx+y{x}^{2}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ is

$$
y={e}^{-4/3}\cdot {e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3}={e}^{({x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-4)/3}\,.
$$

fields.binding: Use the first two non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of ${x}^{-1/2}$ about $x=9$ to approximate the value of ${8}^{-1/2}.$
fields.source_quote:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=9.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{-1/2} \\ f(9) & ={9}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{3} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-3/2} \\ {f}^{′}(9) & =-\frac{1}{2}(9)^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{2\cdot 27}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{-1/2} & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2\cdot 27}(x-9)+⋯ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{x-9}{54}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=8$ into the above to approximate ${8}^{-1/2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{8}^{-1/2} & ≈\frac{1}{3}-\frac{8-9}{54} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{54} \\  & =\frac{19}{54}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding: Which of the following is a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?
fields.source_quote:
A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y)
$$

is said to be homogeneous if it satisfies the following property:

$$
f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)\,
$$

The only option in which this is the case is

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

We can check this using one of two methods.

**Method 1**

Let $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}.$

We see that both the numerator and denominator are homogeneous polynomials of degree $2.$ Therefore, $f(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree $2-2=0.$

Hence, the original differential equation is homogeneous.

**Method 2**

To check this in detail using the definition, we first write:

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}
$$

We can check that this is homogeneous showing that $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(ty)^{2}-(tx)^{2}}{(ty)^{2}+(tx)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}{y}^{2}-{t}^{2}{x}^{2}}{{t}^{2}{y}^{2}+{t}^{2}{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2})}{{t}^{2}({y}^{2}+{x}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ the original differential equation is homogeneous.

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that $cos⁡\theta =\frac{2}{7},$ what is the value of $cot⁡\theta ?$
fields.source_quote:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13932638/assets/8c7889d63cf5894236bc5f5e24feb64ecf5a47acb2c07c807a4e65458a991232.png)

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $sin⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $cos⁡\theta =\frac{2}{7}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{2}{7})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{4}{49}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{45}{49}} \\  & =\pm \frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $sin⁡\theta $ is negative in the fourth quadrant. So, $sin⁡\theta =-\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7}.$

Finally, knowing that $cot⁡\theta =\frac{cos⁡\theta }{sin⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
cot⁡\theta =\frac{(\frac{2}{7})}{(-\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7})}=-\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}=-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{15}.
$$
fields.method: Original unit-circle image shows quadrant IV; full solution uses positive cosine 2/7 and negative sine -3sqrt(5)/7. Their quotient gives the offered complete cotangent -2sqrt(5)/15.

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $y$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\frac{5}{7},$ what is the value of $sec⁡\theta ?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13932638/assets/17e6320115f2cf8b5ffad6abc099169774536af20d2559b453aaa97c1286d96d.png)

We're given that $y=\frac{5}{7}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, $sin⁡\theta =\frac{5}{7}.$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $cos⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{5}{7}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{5}{7})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{25}{49}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{24}{49}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{24}}{7} \\  & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{6}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, knowing that $sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{cos⁡\theta },$ we have

$$

fields.binding: The equation $-4{w}^{2}-4w+11=0$ can be written in the form $4(w+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q,$ and solve the equation.
fields.source_quote:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-4{w}^{2}-4w+11) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 4{w}^{2}+4w-11 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{w}^{2}+4w-11 & =0 \\ 4({w}^{2}+w) & =11 \\ 4[{w}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}w+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}] & =11 \\ 4[{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}] & =11\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-4\cdot \frac{1}{4} & =11 \\ 4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-1 & =11 \\ 4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =11+1 \\ 4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q=12.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =12 \\ {(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{12}{4} \\ {(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =3 \\ \sqrt{{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{3} \\ |w+\frac{1}{2}| & =\sqrt{3} \\ w+\frac{1}{2} & =\pm \sqrt{3} \\ w & =-\frac{1}{2}\pm \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding: The equation $-3{x}^{2}+36x-94=0$ can be written in the form $3(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q-p.$
fields.source_quote:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-3{x}^{2}+36x-94) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-36x+94 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-36x+94 & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-36x & =-94 \\ 3[{x}^{2}-12x] & =-94 \\ 3[{x}^{2}-2\cdot 6x+{6}^{2}-{6}^{2}] & =-94 \\ 3[{(x-6)}^{2}-36] & =-94\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{(x-6)}^{2}-3\cdot 36 & =-94 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2}-108 & =-94 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2} & =-94+108 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2} & =14\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-6$, $q=14.$ Finally,

$$
q-p=14-(-6)=14+6=20.
$$

fields.binding:
Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$O=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].$
fields.source_quote:
First, we find the matrix $\,O-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
O-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is given by $det(O-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $1$st row, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(O-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & -\lambda \end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}0 & -1-\lambda  \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-{\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}+1)+(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ -{\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}+\lambda +2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}+2{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to solve this equation. We find the first root by testing some values. According to the rational zeros theorem, a list of good first guesses consists of all divisors of $2:$ 

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2
$$

Let's pick $x=1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)^{3}+2(1)^{2}-(1)-2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =1$ is a root of the equation. So, we can factor $(\lambda -1)$ out of ${\lambda }^{3}+2{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -2$ using synthetic division:

| $1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-1$ | $-2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $↓$ | $1$ | $3$ | $2$ |
|  | $1$ | $3$ | $2$ | $0$ |

So, we obtain the following factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -1)({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +2) & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda +1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

fields.binding: Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events. Given that $P(B)=\frac{1}{15}$ and $P(A\cup B)=\frac{3}{5},$ find $P(A).$
fields.source_quote:
If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events, then $P(A\cap B)=0.$ 

Therefore, by the addition law, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B) \\ P(A) & =P(A\cup B)-P(B) \\  & =\frac{3}{5}-\frac{1}{15} \\  & =\frac{9-1}{15} \\  & =\frac{8}{15}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+16y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$
fields.source_quote:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+16y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =\pm 4\text{i}$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=P\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x$ because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}=x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x)+4x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x) \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =8(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x)+16x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
8(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x)+16x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x)+16x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x)\,=4\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-8\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+8\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x=4\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡4x) \\ -8\alpha =4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡4x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{1}{2}$, $\beta =0.$
Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}=P\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡4x-\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x.
$$

fields.binding: Find the inverse Laplace transform for $F(s)=\frac{10}{(s-2)(s+3)}.$
fields.source_quote:
First, we write $F(s)$ as a sum of partial fractions, as follows: 

$$
\frac{10}{(s-2)(s+3)}=\frac{2}{s-2}-\frac{2}{s+3}
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{2t}} & =\frac{1}{s-2},\,s>2 \\ L{{e}^{-3t}} & =\frac{1}{s+3},\,s>-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the addition property of the Laplace transform, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{\frac{2}{s-2}-\frac{2}{s+3}} & =2{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-2}}-2{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+3}} \\  & =2{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{-3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the inverse Laplace transform of $F(s)=\frac{10}{(s-2)(s+3)}$ is $f(t)=2{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{-3t}.$

fields.binding: Given that $y=y(x)$ satisfies the equation ${y}^{″}+8{y}^{′}+15y=0,$ which of the following **cannot** be $y(x)?$
fields.source_quote:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+8\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+15{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +15) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +15 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
(\lambda +3)(\lambda +5)=0,
$$

and so the solutions of the auxiliary equation  are $\lambda =-3$ or $\lambda =-5.$

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{-3x}$ and ${e}^{-5x}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only ${e}^{5x}$ is not a solution.

$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=-2\alpha {e}^{-2x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=4\alpha {e}^{-2x}\end{aligned}

Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+36y=-12\operatorname{cos}⁡6x
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡6x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡6x,$ find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
fields.source_quote:
The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x$ because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x)+6x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡6x) \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =12(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡6x)-36x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x)\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
12(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡6x)-36x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x)+36x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x)=-12\operatorname{cos}⁡6x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-12\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡6x+12\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡6x=-12\operatorname{cos}⁡6x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}12\beta =-12\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡6x) \\ -12\alpha =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡6x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =0$ and $\beta =-1.$ Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡6x.
$$

fields.binding:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=-2{x}^{2}-4x+3
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-2x}+Bx{e}^{-2x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
fields.source_quote:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma 
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta ,$ and $\gamma $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x+\beta ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=2\alpha 
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ $\beta $ and $\gamma ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
2\alpha +4(2\alpha x+\beta )+4(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma )=-2{x}^{2}-4x+3
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives:

$$
4\alpha {x}^{2}+(8\alpha +4\beta )x+(2\alpha +4\beta +4\gamma )=-2{x}^{2}-4x+3
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}4\alpha =-2\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ 8\alpha +4\beta =-4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ 2\alpha +4\beta +4\gamma =3\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{1}{2},\beta =0,\gamma =1.$

Therefore, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+1.
$$

fields.binding:
The position $y(t),$ measured in centimeters, of a particle oscillating with forced harmonic motion without damping is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+49y=-24\operatorname{cos}⁡t,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the particle is initially at the origin with zero velocity, find the position of the particle after $\frac{\pi }{2}$ seconds.
fields.source_quote:
The general solution to the equation of forced harmonic motion without damping is the sum of the complementary function and a particular solution.

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ represents simple harmonic motion and can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=49\,⟹\,\omega =7.
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡7t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡7t.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t).$

The external force is $-24\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡t,
$$

where $\alpha ,\beta $ are constants to be determined.

Substituting ${y}_{p}$ into the differential equation and equating coefficients gives $\alpha =-\frac{1}{2},\beta =0.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡7t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡7t-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Since the particle is initially at the origin with zero velocity, the initial conditions are $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=0.$

Solving with these conditions for $A$ and $B$ gives

$$
A=\frac{1}{2},\,B=0.
$$

So our solution is

$$
y(t)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡7t-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

To find the position of the particle after $\frac{\pi }{2}$ seconds, we substitute into the equation $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{2})-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding: Calculate the points where the ellipse ${x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}+6x+6y=3$  intercepts the $x$-axis.
fields.source_quote:
To calculate the $x$-intercepts, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ We do this and solve the resulting equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}+6x+6y & =3 \\ {x}^{2}+3\cdot {0}^{2}+6x+6\cdot 0 & =3 \\ {x}^{2}+6x & =3 \\ (x+3)^{2}-9 & =3 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =3+9 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =12 \\ x+3 & =\pm 2\sqrt{3} \\ x & =-3\pm 2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at $(-3-2\sqrt{3},0)$ and $(-3+2\sqrt{3},0).$

fields.binding: Determine the points where the ellipse $3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6\sqrt{3}x-6y+6=0$ intercepts the $y$-axis.
fields.source_quote:
To calculate the $y$-intercepts, we need to substitute $x=0$ in the equation of the ellipse and try to solve the resulting equation for $y.$ We do this and solve the resulting equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6\sqrt{3}x-6y+6 & =0 \\ 3(0)^{2}+{y}^{2}-6\sqrt{3}(0)-6y+6 & =0 \\ {y}^{2}-6y+6 & =0 \\ (y-3)^{2}-9+6 & =0 \\ (y-3)^{2} & =3 \\ y-3 & =\pm \sqrt{3} \\ y & =3\pm \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,3-\sqrt{3})$ and $(0,3+\sqrt{3}).$

fields.binding: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}]?$
fields.source_quote:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 \\ -2 & -4 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4-\lambda  & -4 \\ -2 & -4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & -4 \\ -4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}0 & 4-\lambda  \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )((4-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-16)-4(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )(20-4\lambda -5\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-16)-4(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +4)-4(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +4-4) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -4)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}0 & 2-\lambda  \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(2-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-(2-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-1) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda (2-\lambda )^{2} & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,2,\,0\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1-\lambda  & 0\end{aligned}|+(1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ -(1-\lambda )+(1-\lambda )[(2-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-1)] & =0 \\ -(1-\lambda )+(1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +1-1) & =0 \\ \lambda (1-\lambda )(\lambda -3) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}

fields.source_quote:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $25{x}^{2}=(5x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{e}^{\pi }}{\sqrt{25{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{{e}^{\pi }}{\sqrt{(5x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{\pi }\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\cdot \frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{5}\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{5}\operatorname{arcosh}⁡5x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding: Let $f(x,y)$ be a function that is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where $a=⟨1,2⟩$ and $b=⟨2,3⟩$ are the position vectors of $A$ and $B,$ respectively. If $f(a)=1$ and $f(b)=6,$ then according to the mean value theorem, which of the following must be true for some point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c?$
fields.source_quote:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(b)-f(a) & =∇f(c)·(b-a) \\ 6-1 & =⟨{f}_{x}(c),{f}_{y}(c)⟩\cdot (⟨2,3⟩-⟨1,2⟩) \\ 5 & =⟨{f}_{x}(c),{f}_{y}(c)⟩\cdot ⟨1,1⟩ \\ 5 & ={f}_{x}(c)+{f}_{y}(c).\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding: Let $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2).$
fields.source_quote:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot ⟨x+1,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & ={e}^{y}\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=2, \\ {f}_{y} & =x{e}^{y} &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-1{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =⟨2,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇\,f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\  & =-2+⟨2,-2⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\  & =-2+2(x+1)-2(y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+2x-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding: Let $f(x,y,z)=xy-\operatorname{ln}⁡z.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1,e).$
fields.source_quote:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1,e)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,1,e)+∇f(1,1,e)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1,z-e⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(1,1,e)=0.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =y\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(1,1,e)=1, \\ {f}_{y} & =x\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(1,1,e)=1, \\ {f}_{z} & =-\frac{1}{z}\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{z}(1,1,e)=-\frac{1}{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(1,1,e)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(1,1,e) & =⟨1,1,-\frac{1}{e}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,1,e)+∇f(1,1,e)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1,z-e⟩ \\  & =0+⟨1,1,-\frac{1}{e}⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1,z-e⟩ \\  & =0+1(x-1)+1(y-1)-\frac{1}{e}(z-e) \\  & =-1+x+y-\frac{z}{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.binding: Let $f(x,y,z)=\frac{9}{x+2y-z}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,1,1).$
fields.source_quote:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,1,1)+∇f(2,1,1)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-1,z-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(2,1,1)=3.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =-\frac{9}{(x+2y-z)^{2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(2,1,1)=-\frac{9}{(2+2(1)-1)^{2}}=-1, \\ {f}_{y} & =-\frac{18}{(x+2y-z)^{2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(2,1,1)=-\frac{18}{(2+2(1)-1)^{2}}=-2, \\ {f}_{z} & =\frac{9}{(x+2y-z)^{2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(2,1,1)=\frac{9}{(2+2(1)-1)^{2}}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(2,1,1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(2,1,1) & =⟨{f}_{x}(2,1,1),{f}_{y}(2,1,1),{f}_{z}(2,1,1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,1,1)+∇f(2,1,1)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-1,z-1⟩ \\  & =3+⟨-1,-2,1⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y-1,z-1⟩ \\  & =3-1(x-2)-2(y-1)+1(z-1) \\  & =6-x-2y+z.\end{aligned}
$$

To apply the ratio test we define ${a}_{n}=\frac{{x}^{n}}{{n}^{3/2}}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{x}^{n+1}}{(n+1)^{3/2}}\cdot \frac{{n}^{3/2}}{{x}^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{n}{n+1})}^{3/2}|x| \\  & =|x|{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{n}{n+1})}^{3/2} \\  & =|x|\cdot 1 \\  & =|x|\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied for $|x|<1.$ So, the radius of convergence is $1,$ and the series converges for any $x$ that lies in the open interval $(-1,1).$

The ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence of the series when $L=1.$ So, when $|x|=1,$ we do not know if the series converges. This means that the endpoints $x=-1$ and $x=1$ need to be investigated separately using another test for convergence.

- When $x=1$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{{n}^{3/2}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{1}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{2}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{3}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{4}^{3/2}}+⋯\,,\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the $p$-series test.  So the endpoint $x=1$ is included in our interval.

- When $x=-1$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{{n}^{3/2}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3/2}} \\  & =-\,\frac{1}{{1}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{2}^{3/2}}-\frac{1}{{3}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{4}^{3/2}}+⋯\,,\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the alternating series test.  So the endpoint $x=-1$ is included in our interval.

Therefore, the interval of convergence is $[-1,1].$
